# Summary: Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer engineer notable for his work in analog and digital computing. Surviving severe wartime injuries and active participation in the Polish resistance, he began his professional career developing the AAH (Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics) and subsequently built AKAT-1 in 1959, the world's first transistor-based differential equations analyzer. His achievements led to a UNESCO scholarship, allowing him to study at leading US research centers, where he met prominent figures like John Eckert and Claude Shannon. Upon returning, Karpiński created one of the world’s first perceptrons in 1964 and designed the KAR-65 computer, Poland’s fastest at the time.
Karpiński’s most ambitious project was the K-202 minicomputer in the early 1970s, a highly innovative machine featuring components such as Intel 4004 chips and advanced memory segmentation. Despite its technical superiority, only 30 units were produced due to administrative barriers and lack of political support. Later in life, Karpiński worked on various ventures in Poland and Switzerland and was recognized with the Officer’s and Commander’s Crosses of Polonia Restituta for his contributions. His legacy is debated due to alleged informant activities and the stifled potential of his creations under communist-era restrictions.
